851.event_title: Florence's Guelfs split into Blacks and Whites and Dante is exiled
851.event: Around 1300 the Guelf party that governed Florence divided into two hostile factions, the Blacks led by Corso Donati and the Whites, to which the poet Dante Alighieri belonged. In 1302 the Blacks, allied with Pope Boniface VIII, took control of the city and expelled the Whites. Dante, who was away on a diplomatic mission, was condemned and banished, and spent the rest of his life in exile, during which he wrote the Divine Comedy.
851.explanation: The feud shows how hostility within a single ruling party could tear a prosperous city apart and drive out even its greatest poet.
851.tie_back: The kural calls hostility a disease that feeds the refusal to live together, and in Florence it split even former allies of one party into factions that could no longer share the city.
851._accuracy_note: Strong illustration of hostility breeding division, though the kural speaks of it in all living beings rather than in politics.

852.event_title: The Greensboro sit-in at the Woolworth lunch counter
852.event: On 1 February 1960 four students from North Carolina A&T, Ezell Blair Jr., Franklin McCain, Joseph McNeil and David Richmond, sat down at the whites-only lunch counter of the Woolworth store in Greensboro and politely asked to be served. When they were refused and asked to leave, they stayed quietly in their seats. Over the following six months hundreds of students and community members joined the protest and a boycott, and the counter was desegregated on 25 July 1960.
852.explanation: The sit-in sparked a wave of nonviolent sit-ins across the South and showed the power of patient, peaceful refusal in the face of injustice.
852.tie_back: The kural teaches that even when others do us wrong, the highest course is not to hurt them in return, and the students answered refusal and exclusion with calm, nonviolent persistence.
852._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit for non-retaliation; the sources consulted document the students' politeness but not specific provocations they endured.

853.event_title: Robert Schuman proposes pooling French and German coal and steel
853.event: On 9 May 1950 French Foreign Minister Robert Schuman proposed that French and German coal and steel production be placed under a common High Authority open to other European countries, so that war between France and Germany would become not merely unthinkable but materially impossible. The proposal led to the Treaty of Paris of 1951, which created the European Coal and Steel Community of six countries. In 1985 the date of the declaration was made Europe Day.
853.explanation: After three wars between France and Germany in seventy years, the declaration began the reconciliation that grew into the European Union, and Schuman is honoured as one of its founders.
853.tie_back: The kural promises unfading renown to those who rid themselves of the disease of hostility, and Schuman's turn away from Franco-German enmity is still commemorated every year on Europe Day.
853._accuracy_note: Strong fit for lasting renown won by ending hostility, though the declaration was a collective policy as much as one man's change of heart.

854.event_title: The Berlin Wall opens and Berliners celebrate
854.event: On the evening of 9 November 1989 an unclear announcement of new travel rules by East German official Gunter Schabowski sent thousands of East Berliners to the border crossings. At Bornholmer Strasse the overwhelmed guards opened the checkpoint, and people poured through to be greeted by West Berliners with flowers and champagne, while others climbed onto the Wall and began chipping pieces from it. More than two million East Berliners visited West Berlin that weekend.
854.explanation: The opening of the Wall ended nearly three decades of division in Berlin and opened the way to German reunification in 1990.
854.tie_back: The kural says that when hostility, the worst of miseries, is destroyed it yields the greatest of joys, and the night the symbol of Cold War enmity was breached became one of the most joyful public celebrations of the century.
854._accuracy_note: Strong on joy following the end of division, though the Wall stood for a political divide more than personal hostility.

855.event_title: Martin Luther King Jr. calms the crowd after his home is bombed
855.event: During the Montgomery bus boycott, Martin Luther King Jr.'s home was bombed on the evening of 30 January 1956 while he was speaking at a mass meeting; his wife Coretta and their baby daughter were unhurt. He returned to find a large, angry crowd, many of them armed, gathered outside and refusing police orders to leave. Standing on his damaged porch, King urged them to love their enemies and to go home calmly, and what could have become a riot ended peacefully.
855.explanation: King's refusal to answer violence with violence kept the boycott nonviolent, and the movement went on to win the desegregation of Montgomery's buses later that year.
855.tie_back: The kural asks who could ever overcome those who turn away from hostility whenever it rises, and King turned himself and his supporters away from retaliation at the very moment it was most provoked, making the movement unbeatable.
855._accuracy_note: Near dramatisation of turning away from rising hostility, with an outcome that matched the kural's promise.

856.event_title: Charles the Bold's wars end in his death at Nancy
856.place: Grandson and Morat, Switzerland; Nancy, Lorraine, France
856.event: Charles the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, pursued constant wars of expansion, and after a failed siege of Neuss he went to war against the Swiss confederates and the Duke of Lorraine. In 1476 the Swiss defeated him at Grandson and again at Morat. On 5 January 1477 he was killed in battle at Nancy against Rene II of Lorraine and his Swiss allies, and his Burgundian state was then divided between the King of France and the Habsburgs.
856.explanation: Within three years of his greatest power, Charles's appetite for war had destroyed both himself and the independent Burgundian state he had sought to enlarge.
856.tie_back: The kural warns that for one who thinks it sweet to get ahead through hostility, failure and ruin are near, and Charles's relentless warring brought defeat, death and the break-up of his realm within a few years.
856._accuracy_note: Strong fit for the swift ruin that follows delight in conflict.

857.event_title: The Royal Society's one-sided verdict in the calculus priority dispute
857.event: After Newton's supporter John Keill suggested in 1708 that Gottfried Leibniz had plagiarised Newton's calculus, Leibniz appealed to the Royal Society, of which Newton was president. Newton chose a committee of his supporters, which published the Commercium Epistolicum in 1712 favouring Newton's priority, and Newton himself wrote an anonymous review of it in the Philosophical Transactions. Historians now credit both men with inventing the calculus independently.
857.explanation: The bitter dispute is remembered as a case in which personal rivalry overrode fair judgement in one of the greatest scientific institutions of the age.
857.tie_back: The kural says those whose minds are bent on hostility cannot see the true principle that leads to success, and the quarrel led even Newton to abandon impartial inquiry in favour of winning the fight.
857._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: it shows hostility distorting judgement, not a clear loss of success for the hostile party.

858.event_title: The Rush-Bagot Agreement disarms the Great Lakes
858.event: Less than three years after the War of 1812, acting U.S. Secretary of State Richard Rush and the British minister Sir Charles Bagot concluded an agreement by exchange of notes limiting naval forces on the Great Lakes and Lake Champlain. Each side was allowed only a few small vessels of no more than 100 tons, each armed with a single 18-pound cannon. The U.S. Senate approved it in April 1818.
858.explanation: The agreement is regarded as one of the most successful disarmament agreements in history and helped lower tensions between the United States and British North America after the war.
858.tie_back: The kural says turning away from hostility brings prosperity while pushing it further invites ruin, and the two former enemies chose to stand down their warships on the lakes rather than continue a naval race.
858._accuracy_note: Strong on turning away from hostility; the sources consulted do not directly document the prosperity that followed.

859.event: After the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, the Austro-Hungarian government in July 1914 drafted an ultimatum to Serbia in terms intended to be impossible to accept, and delivered it on 23 July. Serbia replied on time on 25 July, accepting all but two of the demands and offering international arbitration, but Austria-Hungary declared the reply insufficient and declared war on 28 July. The war that followed ended in 1918 with the collapse of the Habsburg monarchy.
859.explanation: By choosing to escalate rather than accept a largely conciliatory reply, the Habsburg government began the war that destroyed its own empire.
859.tie_back: The kural says that a person heading for ruin looks to magnify hostility, and Austria-Hungary deliberately enlarged a dispute that Serbia had offered to settle, setting off its own downfall.
859._accuracy_note: Strong illustration, though the causes of the First World War involved many states beyond Austria-Hungary.

860.event_title: Argentina and Chile dedicate the Christ of the Andes
860.place: Uspallata (Bermejo) Pass, on the Argentina-Chile border
860.event: Argentina and Chile, long in dispute over their Andean border and preparing for possible war, agreed in 1902 to settle their claims by arbitration and to limit their armaments. The boundary was settled by an arbitral award that both sides accepted. In 1904 the colossal statue known as the Christ of the Andes, sculpted by Mateo Alonso, was dedicated high on the border pass to commemorate the peace and boundary settlements between the two countries.
860.explanation: The settlement turned a likely war into a lasting peace, and the statue became one of the world's best-known monuments to friendship between nations.
860.tie_back: The kural says that from hostility come all painful things while from friendliness comes true goodness, and the two republics chose arbitration and friendship over war, marking the choice with a monument of peace.
860._accuracy_note: Strong fit for the fruits of friendliness over hostility, though some details of the dispute and arbitration vary between sources.
